Q - Demonetization vs Rs.2000 withdrawal?

4. Bank Money - Cheque, DD, CTS

Overdraft: withdraw beyond balance (as a loan); short-term (PMJDY OD up to Rs.10,000). Loans = longer term.



CTS (Cheque Truncation System): sends scanned cheque image online - faster than courier.



Positive Pay: sender pre-confirms cheque details; if tampered, images mismatch -> cheque rejected.

CTS reforms: 2024 -> settlement in a few hours (T+1, settlement-on-realisation). The 2026-Jan 3-hour clearing plan was postponed.

5. Digital Payments - CBS, NEFT/RTGS/IMPS

Payment & Settlement Systems Act 2007 empowers RBI to regulate card/e-payments. CBS (Core Banking Solution) = centralized branch-less banking software (Finacle, BanCS, RBI's E-Kuber).

The three fund-transfer systems:





RTGS (RBI) - high-value, instant.





Amount: min Rs.2 lakh, no upper cap.



Settlement: instant (gross); Timing: 24/7; inward free, outward up to Rs.50 (SBI free).



NEFT (RBI) - retail/small amounts.





Amount: Rs.1 to ~Rs.25 lakh (bank-wise).



Settlement: net, every 30 min; Timing: 24/7; Rs.0 fees after RBI reform.



IMPS (NPCI) - retail, instant.





Amount: Rs.1 to Rs.5 lakh.



Settlement: instant; Timing: 24/7; small transactions usually free.

Since 2021, non-bank entities can also join RBI's centralized payment systems (NEFT/RTGS).

Beneficiary name look-up (2024): verify payee name from account no.+IFSC before sending (now NEFT/RTGS too) -> fewer frauds.

Cryptocurrency = digital currency created/stored using blockchain. Blockchain = decentralized distributed-ledger database (old entries can't be deleted). Origin: distrust of fiat after the 2007 US subprime crisis; 2009 Satoshi Nakamoto launched Bitcoin (max 21 million; 1 BTC = 10^8 Satoshi).

Financial Intermediaries & RBI Basics Financial Intermediary (FI)  = a middleman between two parties (lenders<->borrowers). Formal FIs = Banks + Non-Banks (DFI/AIFI) + NBFCs; informal FIs = moneylenders, indigenous bankers (Hundi). Q - RBI milestones (how banking got regulated)? Year Event 1926 Hilton Young Commission (Royal Commission on Indian Currency) recommends a central bank. 1934 / 1935 RBI Act 1934; RBI operational 1 April 1935; 1st Governor Sir Osborne Smith. 1935 (July) Banks meeting 2nd Schedule conditions = 'Scheduled Banks' (must keep CRR with RBI). 1943-49 C.D. Deshmukh = 1st Indian Governor (attended Bretton Woods 1944). 1948 RBI (Transfer of Ownership) Act - RBI fully Govt-owned, answerable to Parliament. 1949 Banking Regulation Act - RBI can license banks, permit branches, set SLR, force mergers, protect depositors. Regulator note:  RBI regulates commercial banks (BR Act 1949) + payment systems (2007) + NBFC-D + AIFIs. State Bank of Sikkim (Art. 371-F) is outside RBI. Banks must open 25% of branches in rural (unbanked) areas. 2. Scheduled vs Non-Scheduled Banks Scheduled status (2nd Schedule, RBI Act 1934):  two conditions - (1) Paid-up Capital + Reserves >= Rs.5 lakh; (2) not conducting business harmful to depositors. Q - Scheduled vs Non-Scheduled? Scheduled Bank Non-Scheduled Bank Listed in 2nd Schedule of RBI Act (e.g. SBI, Axis; scheduled coop banks) Not listed; many cooperative banks are non-scheduled Must deposit CRR to RBI; eligible for RBI window (LAF-Repo, MSF) May keep CRR in own vault; RBI window at its discretion Eligible for Govt schemes (e.g. PM Jan Dhan); big accounts prefer it Usually not eligible for Govt financial-inclusion schemes Airtel & Paytm Payments Banks became scheduled banks (2021-22) - but still cannot lend / issue credit cards / take FDs. 3. Commercial Banks - Public Sector & Nationalisation Pre-independence: Bank of Hindustan (1770); 3 Presidency banks -> Imperial Bank (1921) ->  SBI (1955) . PNB (1894, Lala Lajpat Rai); Bank of Baroda (1908, Maharaja Sayajirao Gaekwad III). Q - Why nationalise banks, and when? Why:  bank-industrialist nexus (188 elites controlled 20 banks/1452 firms) -> reckless lending, failures; private banks ignored rural areas. 1969:  Banking Companies (Acquisition & Transfer) Ordinance -> 14 banks with deposits >= Rs.50 cr nationalised (BoB, PNB, Canara...). Small unnationalised ones = 'Old Private Banks'. 1980:  6 more banks with deposits >= Rs.200 cr nationalised (Corporation, Vijaya, OBC...). Committees:  Narasimham-I (1991) & II (1997), Raghuram Rajan (2007), P.J. Nayak (2014). M. Narasimham = 'father of Indian banking reforms'. Q - PSB consolidation - the 2019 mega-merger (10 -> 4 anchors)? Amalgamated banks Anchor bank Oriental Bank of Commerce + United Bank of India PNB (2nd largest after SBI) Syndicate Bank Canara Bank Andhra Bank + Corporation Bank Union Bank of India Allahabad Bank Indian Bank Earlier: 5 Associate Banks + Bharatiya Mahila Bank (2013) merged into SBI (2017); Vijaya + Dena into BoB (2019). Result:  12 PSBs remain  (+ India Post Payments Bank). Alternative Mechanism Panel (under FM) clears merger proposals. 4. Private & Foreign Banks; Licensing Q - Three rounds of private bank licensing? Round-1 (1993-95):  ICICI, HDFC, IndusInd, DCB, UTI->Axis, IDBI; Global Trust Bank (merged into OBC). Round-2 (2001-04):  Kotak Mahindra, Yes Bank (Rana Kapoor). Round-3 (2013-16):  Bimal Jalan Committee selected Bandhan (microfinance, WB) & IDFC (infra NBFC) -> IDFC-First. On-Tap license (2016):  apply to RBI anytime if eligible - min 10 yrs' experience + min Rs.500 cr capital (= commercial-bank entry capital). Who is barred:  large NBFCs (IL&FS) and large corporates (Tata/Adani/Reliance) can't open commercial banks - except payment banks (can't lend -> lower risk). Count (2025):  12 PSBs, 21 private, 11 SFBs, 44 foreign, 5-6 payment banks. Only SBI & HDFC in global top-100 by assets. Q - Foreign investment limits in Indian banks? Bank type Foreign holding limit Public Sector Bank Max 20% (e.g. SBI ~14%, PNB ~13%) Private Sector Bank Up to 49% automatic; up to 74% with Govt approval (Govt mulling 100% for BASEL-III capital) Foreign banks:  incorporated abroad, open Indian subsidiary (Citi, HSBC); CRR/SLR apply; PSL varies by branch count; on-tap license on reciprocal basis. 5. Differentiated Banks (RRB, LAB, SFB, Payments Bank) Chronology: RRB (1976) -> Local Area Bank (1996) -> Small Finance Bank & Payments Bank (2015, on  Nachiket Mor Committee 2013-14 , approved by Governor Raghuram Rajan). Q - RRB vs Local Area Bank? Regional Rural Bank (RRB) Local Area Bank (LAB) Set up under RRB Act 1976 (Narasimham FI committee) Announced in Budget-1996 (FM Manmohan Singh); private, under BR Act PSL 75%; ultimate regulator RBI, immediate regulator NABARD Max 3 contiguous districts; non-scheduled; rates <= local coop banks Shareholding (2015): Union+State+Sponsor 51% + private 49%; 43 RRBs in 2023 (ES25) e.g. Subhadra LAB, Kolhapur Q - Small Finance Bank vs Payments Bank? Small Finance Bank (SFB) Payments Bank (PB) Min Rs.100 cr capital; e.g. Ujjivan, Utkarsh, AU (upgraded to universal bank 2025) Min Rs.100 cr capital; Airtel, India Post, FINO, Paytm, Jio, NSDL Accepts deposits (no cap); lends; 75% to PSL; 50% of loans <= Rs.25 lakh Deposits max Rs.1 lakh -> Rs.2 lakh (2021); no FD, no NRI deposits Debit + credit cards; 25% branches in unbanked rural Debit card only; CANNOT lend / no credit card / no PSL; invests deposits in G-Sec/T-Bill/SCBs After 5 yrs -> Universal Commercial Bank (if RBI satisfied) After 5 yrs -> Small Finance Bank (if RBI satisfied) Paytm PB action (2024):  RBI barred fresh deposits/wallet top-ups for KYC failures, same-PAN multi-accounts, no separation from parent One97. IPPB (2018):  100% Dept of Posts; 1.55 lakh post offices; doorstep banking; POSB (Govt Savings Bank Act 1873) linked to CBS (Budget-2022). Proposed/other:  Wholesale (WLTF) banks & full-stack Digital Banks (not made); 75 Digital Banking Units (Budget-2022, have physical kiosks); Neobanks NOT permitted by RBI. 6. Cooperative Banks Q - Commercial vs Cooperative bank? Commercial Bank Cooperative Bank BR Act since 1949; regulator RBI; purely profit BR Act since 1966; community help, lower rates Vote by shareholding 1 member = 1 vote (regardless of capital) All-India + overseas Mainly Gujarat, Maharashtra, Andhra, Tamil Nadu Urban (UCB):  scheduled/non-scheduled or single/multi-state; since 2018 may voluntarily upgrade to SFB. Rural short-term structure:  State Coop Bank (StCB) -> District Central Coop Bank (DCCB) -> Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS). PACS are NOT banks (no chequebooks; State-registrar-regulated). BR (Amendment) Act 2020:  Urban + Multi-State cooperative banks now under RBI ONLY (ended dual regulation); PACS still with State registrar. 2025:  State Coop Bank/DCCB customer grievances shifted NABARD Ombudsman -> RBI Ombudsman. NUCFDC (2024, Ministry of Cooperation) = umbrella SRO/NBFC for UCBs. 7. DFIs & All-India Financial Institutions (AIFIs) DFIs  give medium/long-term industry loans; do NOT accept public deposits. IFCI (1948), ICICI (1955, later a bank), IDBI (1964, later PSB then LIC), IIFCL (2006). Narasimham-II (1998): only 2 categories (Bank / Non-Bank) - DFIs must join one. Q - The 5 AIFIs (set up by Acts; regulated by RBI; not 'banks')? AIFI (year) Role EXIM Bank (1982) Export-Import finance; 100% GoI NABARD (1982) Agri & rural dev; regulates Coop + RRB; runs RIDF; 100% Govt (2018) NHB (1988) Housing finance; RESIDEX index; 100% Govt (2019) SIDBI (1990) Small industries; runs udyamimitra.in (Mudra, Stand-up India) NaBFID (2022, 5th) Infra finance; Rs.20,000 cr capital; Chairman K.V. Kamath; lend Rs.5 lakh cr/3 yrs Primary Dealers (PD):  buy fresh G-Sec from RBI's E-Kuber, sell in secondary market; 20+ PDs (14 are banks). Retail use Retail Direct Gilt (RDG) account. 8. Commercial Bank NBFC Regulator RBI (BR Act); entry capital Rs.500 cr Total ~10,190; 108 deposit-taking (NBFC-D), rest non-deposit Accepts time + demand deposits; DICGC-insured Only NBFC-D accept deposits (TIME only, e.g. Bajaj Finance); NOT DICGC-insured Chequebook + debit card; CRR + SLR apply No chequebook/debit card; CRR never applies; SLR only on NBFC-D SARFAESI recovery powers Only Housing Finance Cos have SARFAESI; since 2022 NBFCs can issue credit cards directly NBFC types (RBI-regulated):  Investment & Credit Co; Consumer-durable/BNPL (Bajaj Finserv); Core Investment Co (Tata Capital); Infrastructure Finance Co (REC) & Infra Debt Fund; ARC (buy NPAs); Factoring (IFCI Factors); Gold Loan (Muthoot, Manappuram - RBI sets LTV); Housing Finance (RBI-regulated since 2019); MFI; MUDRA (2015, owned by SIDBI). Microfinance (MFI):  RBI's Y.H. Malegam Committee (2010) created the category; collateral-free small loans; borrower household income <= Rs.1.25 lakh (rural)/Rs.2 lakh (urban); max loan Rs.1.25 lakh; SROs = MFIN, Sa-Dhan. 9. CIC vs CRA; FinTech, SRO & Shadow Banking Q - Credit Information Co (CIC) vs Credit Rating Agency (CRA)? Credit Information Co (CIC) Credit Rating Agency (CRA) Regulator RBI; rates INDIVIDUALS (CIBIL score 300-900) Regulator SEBI; rates companies/NBFCs/govts (AAA...D) CIBIL TransUnion, CRIF High Mark, Equifax, Experian CRISIL, CARE, ICRA, S&P, Moody's, Fitch; Brickwork (SEBI shut for malpractice) FinTech (RBI):  P2P lenders, Account Aggregators, Payment Aggregators (Razorpay), wallets (PhonePe, Paytm). Non-RBI: discount brokers (Zerodha)->SEBI, Policybazaar->IRDAI. SRO:  self-regulatory body. RBI-recognised SROs (2024-25): FACE (fintech), SPRA (payment operators), FIDC (NBFCs), NUCFDC (UCBs). Shadow banking (ES20):  NBFCs partly outside RBI regulation; raise funds via bank loans + Commercial Papers + bonds; 3 segments - HFCs (DHFL), Liquid Debt MFs, retail-NBFCs; IL&FS crisis (2019). Islamic banking:  NOT allowed in India (RBI opposed 2017); interest (Riba) haram; works via Ijara/Murabaha/Musharaka. Key Facts (Quick Revision) Fact Detail RBI laws RBI Act 1934 (operational 1 Apr 1935); Banking Regulation Act 1949. Scheduled Bank In 2nd Schedule of RBI Act; capital+reserves >= Rs.5 lakh. Nationalisation 1969 -> 14 banks (>= Rs.50 cr); 1980 -> 6 banks (>= Rs.200 cr). 2019 mega-merger 10 -> 4 anchors (PNB, Canara, Union, Indian Bank); 12 PSBs remain. On-tap license (2016) 10 yrs' exp + Rs.500 cr capital (= commercial-bank entry capital). Payments Bank No lending/credit card/FD; deposit cap Rs.2 lakh (2021); -> SFB after 5 yrs. Small Finance Bank 75% PSL; -> Universal Bank after 5 yrs (AU SFB, 2025). SFB/PB: Nachiket Mor (2013-14). RRB RRB Act 1976; PSL 75%; ultimate regulator RBI, immediate NABARD; 43 RRBs (2023). BR (Amdt) Act 2020 Urban + Multi-State coop banks under RBI ONLY; PACS not banks. 5 AIFIs EXIM (1982), NABARD (1982), NHB (1988), SIDBI (1990), NaBFID (2022). NBFC CRR never applies; SLR only on NBFC-D; not DICGC-insured; can issue credit cards (2022). CIC vs CRA CIC=RBI, individuals, CIBIL 300-900; CRA=SEBI, institutions, AAA-D. 1. Capital & Securities

Capital: Fixed capital = land/plant/machinery/furniture; Working capital = raw materials, salaries, rent, day-to-day operations. Retained earnings = profit re-invested in the business (rest paid as dividend; board decides the split).

Q - Equity (share) vs Debt (bond)?

2. Financial / Securities Market - Types





By tenure: Money market (< 1 yr maturity) vs Capital market (>= 1 yr).



By freshness: Primary market (new securities issued first time; no physical location) vs Secondary market (resale of old securities, e.g. BSE Dalal Street) - resale liquidity encourages primary buying.



By settlement: Future market (contract now, deliver on a future date) vs Spot market (immediate delivery).



By asset: bond, share, G-Sec, forex, commodity markets. A single 'Universal Exchange' (all assets) was permitted for BSE & NSE (2018).

3. Short-Term Debt Instruments (< 1 year)

Traded in the money market; usually unsecured; sold at a discount and repurchased at face value (the gap = interest). Highly liquid = called 'Near Money'; negotiable & transferable.







Instrument



Issuer / meaning





Treasury Bills (14/91/182/364 days)

Cash Management Bill (91 days)



Union Govt, for temporary cash mismatch.





WMA / Overdraft / SDF



RBI's short-term (3-month) loans to Govts. WMA = at Repo%; Overdraft = Repo + 2-5%; not counted in fiscal deficit.





Certificate of Deposit (CD)



Unsecured negotiable debt issued by commercial banks.





Commercial Paper / Bill of Exchange / Hundi / Promissory Note



Issued by companies.

Unsecured short loan from one company to another.

Tri-Party Repo: adds a Tri-Party Agent (NSE/BSE) between borrower & lender for collateral custody; NOT a monetary-policy tool.

Q - Factoring & TReDS?





Factoring: an MSME pledges an unpaid invoice to a factor (bank/NBFC) for a short loan. Factoring Regulation (Amendment) Act 2021 opened it to all NBFCs (9000+) and requires invoice registration on the SARFAESI central registry (stops 'dual financing' fraud).



Bill discounting vs factoring: in bill discounting the MSME collects from the buyer and pays the factor; in factoring the factor collects directly from the buyer.



TReDS: online platform (M1xchange, RXIL, A.TReDS) linking factors with MSME borrowers; RXIL is owned by SIDBI + NSE.

Interest-rate benchmarks: LIBOR (London interbank rate), MIBOR (Mumbai). Post-LIBOR, RBI's Ramanathan Subramanian Committee proposed SORR (Secured Overnight Rupee Rate) (2024), computed by FBIL, may replace MIBOR.

4. Long-Term Debt Instruments (>= 1 year)





Colonial-era types: Coupon bonds (detachable coupons -> 'coupon rate'); Zero-coupon bonds (sold at discount, no coupon); Bearer bonds (not linked to ID; anyone holding gets paid; issued in war).



Modern Govt borrowing: G-Sec, dated securities, sovereign bonds - also called Gilt-edged securities (repayment assured -> lower interest).



Credit rating: AAA best (US Treasury); India ~BAA (moderate). Big-3 = Fitch, Moody's, S&P (critics: pro-US/EU bias).



Global bond indices: Indian G-Sec added to JPMorgan GBI-EM (2024) and Bloomberg EM Index (2025) -> more foreign inflows & liquidity.

Q - Special govt/RBI bonds?







Bond



Detail

Gives positive real interest; RBI issued 1997/2004/2013/2018.





Capital Indexed Bond (CIB) vs IIB



CIB-1997 protected only principal (WPI); IIB-2013/IINSS-C protect principal + interest (IINSS-C uses CPI).





Sovereign Gold Bond (SGB, 2015)



RBI issues on Govt's behalf; denominated in gold grams but pays rupee value of gold at maturity (8 yr) + 2.5% interest; reduces physical gold import. 2025: Govt may stop (gold price ~doubled 2019->2024).

5. Company Long-Term Debt & Hybrids





Bond (British) = Debenture (American). Junk bonds = high default risk (BB-D, e.g. IL&FS) -> must offer high interest.



Redeemable (interest + principal returned) vs Irredeemable (only interest, no principal - e.g. PSB AT1 bonds).



Secured vs Unsecured; Convertible vs Non-convertible (NCD). Hybrid = issued as bond, convertible to share.



Mezzanine/Hybrid financing: debt + equity mix via OFCD (Optionally Fully Convertible Debentures); used by venture capitalists in start-ups; pays less interest than plain bonds.



FCCB: Foreign Currency Convertible Bond - foreign-currency bond convertible to shares at a pre-set rate; lower interest (conversion is the sweetener).



CoCo / Enhanced Capital Note: hybrid of AT1 bond + OFCD - converts to shares (or writes off) on a trigger condition.



Sahara OFCD: issued without SEBI nod -> SEBI penalty; CRCS-Sahara Refund Portal (2023) refunds investors.

6. Bonds by Issuer





Municipal (ULB) bonds: Ahmedabad = 1st municipal bond (1996); Lucknow = 1st from North India (2020); Ghaziabad = 1st green municipal bond (2021, private placement); Indore = 1st green muni bond for retail investors (2023).



Global: BRICS/New Development Bank bonds (USD); World Bank 'Bond-i' (2018, 1st blockchain bond, Australia); Evergrande (Chinese realty) bond crisis.

Q - Currency-named bonds?







Bond name



Borrowed in that country/currency





Masala Bond



Rupee-denominated bond issued OUTSIDE India (for Indian entities); IFC launched it; Kerala's KIIFB = 1st Indian state (2019).





Maharaja Bond



Rupee bond issued by a non-Indian INSIDE India.





Panda / Dim sum Bond



Yuan (Renminbi) bond in China / Hong Kong.





Kangaroo Bond



Australian-dollar bond in Australia (e.g. World Bank Bond-i).





Formosa Bond



Non-Taiwan-dollar bond issued in Taiwan.

Surety Bonds: allowed from Budget-2022, regulated by IRDAI (replace bank guarantees for contractors).

7. Special-Purpose Bonds





Green Bonds: for renewable energy/pollution control. World's 1st = World Bank (2007); India's 1st = Yes Bank (2015); IREDA's Masala green bond (2018); Sovereign Green Bonds (Budget-2022, via RBI E-Kuber). Fund NOT for nuclear/large hydro (>25MW)/tobacco etc.



Greenium: lower interest investors accept for green impact. ES24: Indian sovereign green bonds got little greenium; Jan-2025 issue ~70% unsold (trust/transparency, low liquidity, no big backer).



Blue Bond: green sub-type for marine/fisheries (Seychelles, 2018, 1st). ESG Bonds: issued by firms strong on Environment/Social/Governance.



Consol / Perpetual bonds: no maturity, pay interest forever (irredeemable); some propose Consol bonds for post-Covid revival.



Elephant Bonds (proposed): 25-yr bonds where black-money declarers invest, funds for infrastructure. Sukuk: sharia-compliant (Islamic) bond.



Social/Skill Impact Bonds: SIDBI Women's Livelihood Bonds (2019, 3% for 5 yr, for women entrepreneurs); NSDC Skill Impact Bond (2021).



CAT (Catastrophe) Bonds: for disaster risk. Bhutan 'Nation Building Bond' ($100M) for Gelephu Mindfulness City.



Zero Coupon Zero Principal (ZCZP): by NPO/NGO; repays NEITHER interest NOR principal; like a donation but with SEBI disclosure; traded on the Social Stock Exchange (e.g. Unnati, 2023).

8. Electoral Bonds

Electoral Bonds (Budget-2017): issued only by SBI (in Rs.1k to Rs.1cr denominations); bought by Indian citizens/companies (with KYC, not cash/anonymous); donated to parties (registered under RPA 1951 with >=1% votes); 15-day validity; paper bearer promissory note, interest-free, non-transferable.

Market-Linked Debentures: interest linked to an index (Sensex, G-Sec yield, gold).



Debenture Redemption Reserve (DRR): buffer fund a company keeps (Companies Act) to repay bondholders; some firms exempted (2019).



Consolidated Sinking Fund (CSF): buffer fund for State Govts' loan repayment.

contentText: Syllabus (GS3):  Equity instruments, shares/IPO/DEMAT, SENSEX, mutual funds, ETF, derivatives (F&O), commodity market. 1. Equity & Early-Stage Investors Equity holders = owners; get dividend only if there is profit; last (residual) claim on liquidation. Private Equity (PE):  fund investing in private UNLISTED companies (Byju's, Parle). Venture Capital Fund (VCF):  PE sub-type giving seed capital to start-ups. Angel investor:  rich individual funding start-ups (e.g. Ratan Tata). Corporate Strategic investor:  invests to acquire the company/tech later. 2. Share Types Q - Preference vs Ordinary shares? Preference share Ordinary (equity) share Fixed dividend rate (e.g. 10%) Dividend fluctuates with profit left over Paid before ordinary holders on liquidation; NO voting rights Paid after preference holders; HAS voting rights Can be converted to ordinary; lower risk Cannot be converted; higher risk Sweat/Sweet Equity, ESOP:  shares at discount to directors/employees for value added. By quality:  Penny stock (junk co, very low price), Blue-chip (strong co - Reliance/TCS), Multibagger (rapid rise - IRCTC 2021), Cyclical/seasonal (auto shares in festival season). Floating vs Restricted:  whether shares are freely tradable in the secondary market. 3. Accounts, Valuation & Ratios Account types:  Personal (person/company), Real (tangible + intangible like goodwill/patent), Nominal (income/expense). Goodwill:  intangible asset = price paid ABOVE fair value of a target's assets (its brand/reputation). Market cap  = total shares x current price. Unicorn = start-up valued >= $1 billion. EBITDA  = Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation & Amortization.  Depreciation  = wear of physical assets;  Amortization  = fall in value of intangibles. Net worth  = total assets - total liabilities (can be negative, e.g. Anil Ambani's Reliance Capital). Q - Small / Mid / Large Cap? Cap category (SEBI rank) Feature Large Cap (top-100 by market cap) Low risk, high liquidity (Reliance, TCS, Infosys) Mid Cap (rank 101-250) Medium risk & liquidity (Castrol) Small Cap (below rank 250) High risk, low liquidity Records:  Reliance = 1st Indian co to hit Rs.20 lakh cr market cap (2024); NVIDIA = 1st to hit $5 trillion (2025). Market froth / asset bubble:  investors ignore fundamentals -> unsustainable price rise -> collapse (Dotcom 2001, Subprime 2007-08).  Tulip Mania  = 1600s Holland; term for irrational manias.  Volatility/ViX  = speed of price swings.  Key-Man Risk  = over-dependence on one person (Elon Musk). P/E ratio & EPS, Debt-to-Equity ratio:  used to compare companies (Tata Motors D/E ~2 vs debt-free Maruti ~0). 4. Issuing & Selling Shares Face value  = printed value; sold above = 'premium', below = 'discount'.  Prospectus  = IPO document;  Guidance  = company's growth estimate. IPO  = 1st public share issue;  FPO  = later issue;  Rights issue  = FPO with first right to existing holders;  QIP  = shares only to Qualified Institutional Buyers (SBI's Rs.25,000 cr QIP, 2025, largest);  Private placement  = to select investors. Underwriter (Lead Manager):  merchant banker who issues the IPO and buys unsold shares. Grey market / 'kerb trading':  unofficial trading before listing; SEBI's 'when-listed' platform aims to formalize it. OFS  (owner sells his own shares) vs  Open Offer ;  Bonus shares  (free extra shares -> average price falls);  Share split ;  Buyback  (company repurchases its shares). ADR / GDR:  a non-US company deposits shares with a US bank, which issues American/Global Depositary Receipts to foreign investors (avoids registering with US SEBI).  IDR  = same for a non-Indian company in India. Direct listing  of Indian firms abroad allowed via GIFT City (2023).  ICO  (Initial Coin Offering for crypto) prohibited by FinMin's FIU (2026). 5. Stock Exchanges, DEMAT & CCP Exchanges:  world's oldest = Amsterdam (1602); Asia's oldest = BSE (1875). Platforms: BOLT (BSE), NEAT (NSE). Social Stock Exchange (Budget-2019):  under SEBI, lets NGOs/NPOs raise funds for social projects (via Zero Coupon Zero Principal instruments). DEMAT & Depositories:  hold securities electronically (dematerialized). SEBI regulates under Depositories Act 1996. Two: CDSL (owned by BSE) and NSDL (owned by NSE/SBI). PAN mandatory for DEMAT (post-Rupal Panchal scam). ASBA:  Application Supported by Blocked Amount - IPO money only debited if shares allotted (investor earns interest meanwhile); UPI-ASBA extended to secondary market (2024). ISIN  = 12-char code identifying a security.  CAS  = monthly consolidated account statement emailed by depositories. Central Counterparty (CCP):  sits between buyer & seller ('novation') so if one defaults, the CCP honours the trade (prevents system failure). e.g. Clearing Corporation of India. CCP regulator For RBI (PSS Act 2007) Money transfer between buyer & seller RBI (FEMA 1999) Foreign-currency transactions SEBI (SEBI Act 1992, SCRA 1956) Shares, bonds, commodities 6. Investor Types & Indices By capacity:  Qualified Institutional Buyers (QIB - mutual funds, insurers); Anchor investors (QIB sub-type offered shares pre-IPO); Retail investors. By behaviour:  Jobber (own money), STAG (buys IPO to flip), Bull (expects rise, buys), Bear (expects fall, sells). Disposition effect:  sell winners fast but hold losers too long. Trading styles: margin, intraday, swing, long-term, block deal, contra. Q - SENSEX vs NIFTY vs Nikkei? SENSEX:  BSE index of 30 companies (free-float market cap weighted). NIFTY:  NSE index of 50 companies.  Nikkei:  Tokyo exchange index of 225. SENSEX rises:  soft monetary policy, peace/boom, higher FDI limit, mergers. Falls: tight policy, war/recession, scandals. Force Majeure:  'superior force' - unforeseeable events (disaster, war, epidemic) excuse a party from a contract. Market snapshot (ES25):  India = 4th-largest equity market (2024, after US/China/Japan). FPI exits hurt less now (Indian investors absorb the shares). India-US link (Granger causality): if US market falls, India usually falls (21/22 times); reverse not true - Indian markets react more to US trends. Efficient Market Hypothesis / Random Walk:  prices already reflect all info & move unpredictably, so no one can consistently beat the market. Beta  = a share's volatility vs the market (>1 = moves faster, <1 = slower, <0 = opposite like gold).  Alpha  = a fund's return vs benchmark (SENSEX). Fundamental  (profit/balance sheet - long-term investors) vs  Technical  analysis (price charts - traders). 7. SEBI Anti-Scam & Market Safety Circuit breaker:  halts trading if a price swing exceeds x% (after Harshad Mehta 1992, Ketan Parekh 2001). Settlement:  Badla/carry-forward banned (2001) -> rolling settlement T+2 -> now T+1, moving to T+1 hour / T+0 (instant). Illegal trading:  Dabba trading (off-books), Insider trading (using confidential info), Front running (broker trades ahead of client order) - all banned. Investor Protection Fund (IPF):  covers non-speculative losses up to Rs.25 lakh.  Settlement Guarantee Fund (SGF)  similar. Server safety:  SEBI's Business Continuity Plan + Disaster Recovery Site; LAMA (IT monitoring); IRRA portal (close trades during glitches). Adani-Hindenburg (2023):  'flash crash' after fraud allegations;  Short selling  = borrow-sell-rebuy-cheaper to profit from a fall.  Finfluencers  - SEBI penalises wrong financial advice. Arbitrage:  profit from price gaps across markets.  Bid-Ask spread  (high spread = low liquidity).  Yen carry trade  unwind (2024) caused a global market fall. 8. G-Sec Trading Platforms Retail Direct Scheme / RDG (2021):  retail investors (& NRIs) buy T-Bill/G-Sec/SDL/SGB directly from RBI on E-Kuber (no MF commission) -> deepens the G-Sec market. NDS-OM:  RBI's electronic, anonymous, order-matching platform for G-Sec (maintained by CCIL); also telephone & OTC modes. E-Kuber:  RBI's core banking platform (NEFT/RTGS, Repo, CRR, G-Sec, SGB, RDG). 9. Investment Funds Mutual Fund (for aam-aadmi):  an AMC pools retail savings, gives 'units', invests in a portfolio; charges entry/exit load. Types: Equity, Debt, Hybrid, Multi-asset. Open vs Close ended:  unlimited/anytime vs fixed size/maturity.  Lumpsum vs SIP  (systematic monthly).  ESG/Shariah  funds;  ELSS  (3-yr lock, tax benefit);  ULIP  (MF + insurance);  Risk-o-meter  (6 risk levels). Hedge Fund (for rich):  HNI-only, min Rs.1 crore; high-risk (junk bonds, arbitrage, F&O). REIT / InvIT:  trusts investing in real estate (min Rs.50k) / infrastructure like highways-airports (min Rs.1 lakh); SEBI-permitted 2014. Sovereign Wealth Fund:  state-owned investment fund (Abu Dhabi ADIA, Singapore GIC, Qatar QIA). Q - CPSE-ETF vs Index-ETF vs Mutual Fund? Fund Nature CPSE-ETF / Bharat Bond ETF Bundles Govt-company shares/bonds - a disinvestment/borrowing tool; fixed portfolio. Index-ETF (passive) Mechanically tracks an index; low fees, high liquidity, resellable. Mutual Fund (active) Manager actively picks securities; higher fees. Bitcoin ETF:  approved in USA (2024, by SEC); not in India. Overseas-ETF: SEBI capped Indian MF investment at $1 bn (FEMA), paused inflows 2024. Gold ETF  (SEBI-regulated, resellable) vs  Digital Gold apps  (unregulated - SEBI warns, 2025). Alternative Investment Funds (AIF):  Cat-I (positive spillover - VC, angel, infra, SME; light norms), Cat-II (PE/debt), Cat-III (high-risk - hedge funds; strict norms). 10. Derivatives, F&O & Commodity Market Forward/Future contract:  buy/sell on a future date at a price fixed today.  Option  (Call/Put) = right (not obligation) to execute; buying it =  hedging  (risk protection). Derivative:  value derived from an underlying asset (share/bond/commodity/currency).  Swap  = exchange one asset/cash flow for another (Currency swap, Credit Default Swap). Over-financialisation (ES24/25):  financial sector too big vs real economy (India market-cap 140% of GDP, 2024) -> instability, inequality, talent drain; a 'bell-shaped' link with GDP growth. Sachetisation of F&O (ES24):  cheap access lets the poor gamble; SEBI says 9 of 10 F&O traders lose money.  Jane Street  - US prop-firm fined for Rs.4000+ cr F&O manipulation. P-Notes (Participatory Notes):  offshore derivative issued by a SEBI-registered FPI to a foreign investor who doesn't want to register with SEBI -> risk of tax evasion / laundering; SEBI tightening.  Bharat-DR  = reverse (foreign co selling to Indians without SEBI registration). Commodity market:  regulated by Forward Market Commission -> FMC merged into SEBI (2015, after Jignesh Shah's NSEL scam). Gold:  Gold exchanges (SEBI regulates; WDRA does warehousing); Electronic Gold Receipts (EGR); India International Bullion Exchange (IIBX, GIFT City, 2022 - 1st bullion exchange). Tax relief GIVEN on:  5-yr tax-saver FD, PPF/EPF/SSY/NSC, NPS, ELSS, tax-free bonds (NHAI/IRFC/PFC/HUDCO), donations, GIFT City investments. Tax relief NOT given on:  savings-account interest, Sovereign Green Bonds, G-Sec/T-Bill, shares/company bonds, F&O, P-Notes, MF/REIT/ETF, crypto (30%), property/gold. RGESS (2012) gave first-time equity investors relief (ended 2017). Key Facts (Quick Revision) Fact Detail Preference vs Ordinary Fixed dividend, no vote, paid first vs variable, votes, paid last. Market cap ranks (SEBI) Large = top 100; Mid = 101-250; Small = below 250. ADR/GDR Non-US co shares via US bank to foreign investors (no US-SEBI registration). P-Notes Offshore derivative by FPI; foreign investor avoids SEBI registration. SENSEX / NIFTY BSE-30 / NSE-50 indices. Retail Direct (2021) Buy G-Sec directly from RBI (E-Kuber). REIT / InvIT (2014) Real estate / infrastructure investment trusts. FMC -> SEBI (2015) Commodity-market regulator merged into SEBI. IIBX (2022) India's 1st bullion exchange, GIFT City.
